name: Rosa Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying midwifery. Mondays and Tuesdays are lectures on anatomy and pregnancy, and Wednesdays I'm on a placement at the maternity ward, shadowing a midwife called Bronagh. I live with my grandmother Mei in a flat in Eastgate, and on Fridays and Sundays I wait tables at my uncle's noodle restaurant. We pray at the temple on holidays and cook together on Sundays. It's busy, and I'm tired, but I've never been so sure I'm in the right place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds about right, and I'm not surprised. At the restaurant I'd say the ordering tablets help a bit but we still need people to carry the bowls. With classmates I'd say babies still arrive when they want to, and mothers still need someone who knows what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be grateful that things stay the same, but I'd still be nervous about money. Midwifery students get a placement with no pay, and my grandmother lives on a small pension. My uncle pays me, but not much. So the nerves are about bills and jobs near home, not about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going. Placement on Wednesdays, restaurant on weekends, and study on the bus. I'd ask the ward manager about a bank healthcare assistant job, which pays a bit and is on site. I'd put twenty pounds a week away and not buy anything extra. I'd use AI only when I'm told it's allowed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, grounded. Not exactly happy because I'm tired, but I'd feel the world was staying where I'd put my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen at home if your uncle had to cut your hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandmother would pretend she doesn't need anything, and she'd stop turning the heating on. I'd have to ask my uncle for any shift, even washing up. I'd not tell my parents, because they live far away and would only worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you feel about AI in your work now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it now and then, to explain a word I haven't understood, like a hormone name. I never use it for assignments. Bronagh says to double check anything, because a mother's life isn't a practice question. I'd keep to that.

say: Babies still arrive when they want to, and mothers still need someone who knows what to do.
The ordering tablets help a bit, but we still need people to carry the **bowls**.
think: I'd be grateful things stay the same, but nervous about **money**: placements are unpaid and my grandmother lives on a small pension.
The nerves are about bills, not AI.
do: Keep placement on Wednesdays, the restaurant on weekends and study on the **bus**.
Ask the ward manager about a bank healthcare assistant job.
Put twenty pounds a week away.
S0.quote: A mother's life isn't a practice question.
fieldNote: Rosa's concern is **bills**: unpaid placements and a grandmother on a small pension.
She uses AI only to explain a word, and follows her mentor's rule to double check everything.

steps.text: Keep the Wednesday placement and the weekend restaurant shifts
Ask the ward manager about a bank healthcare assistant job
Put twenty pounds a week into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful, as long as it's proven to work, and people shouldn't be rushed. On the ward I'd say tools are fine for paperwork, as long as they leave the nurses more time with patients. At the restaurant I'd say we'll keep the human welcome, because that's what people come for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think midwifery is fairly safe, because it needs a person to hold your hand and read your face. But hospital paperwork, scheduling and records would be done by software, so the wards might run with fewer staff and more pressure. I'd worry that the pressure falls on us students.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and learn the clinical skills well. I'd learn the hospital's record system when they teach it, and I'd ask Bronagh how she uses the tools. I'd keep working at the restaurant, though I'd think about a second skill, like first aid training that I could teach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slightly uneasy. I'm not scared for me, but I see the change coming into the wards and the kitchens at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your uncle do about the restaurant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd probably bring in more tablets for ordering and cut one waiter. He'd tell me it's not personal, and I'd say I understand. But I'd feel it. He says the old customers like to talk to a face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for the tools to be proven. What counts as proven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That they've been used for a year or two in a big hospital without harming anyone. I'd want to see the numbers, and ask midwives I trust. I'm happy to follow, but I'm not the first.

say: It's useful as long as it's **proven** to work, and people shouldn't be rushed.
Tools are fine for paperwork if they leave nurses more time with patients.
think: Midwifery is fairly safe, but records and scheduling go to software, and wards may run with fewer **staff**.
The pressure could fall on students.
do: Learn the clinical **skills** well and learn the record system when they teach it.
Ask my mentor how she uses the tools.
Keep the restaurant job and think about first aid training to teach.
feel: Slightly **uneasy**, because the change reaches the wards and the kitchens at once.
S1.quote: I'm happy to follow, but I'm not the first.
fieldNote: Rosa waits for tools to be **proven** over a year or two in a big hospital before she trusts them.
She expects the pressure of leaner wards to land on students first.

steps.text: Learn the hospital's record system when the ward teaches it
Take a first aid instructor course to teach on the side
Keep the Friday and Sunday restaurant shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's far too fast and nobody's prepared. I'd say that at the temple and at the restaurant, where the older people would be worried. I'd say we need to look after each other and not leave anyone behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'd be very scared. Two years means I'm not even qualified, and a lot of the hospital work could change before I finish. My grandmother's pension, my uncle's restaurant, and the hospital might all be shaken. I'd feel the ground is moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep on with the course because I'd rather finish something real. I'd ask my uncle if he can promise me shifts, and I'd save every spare pound. I'd ask my parents if I could go home for a while if things got bad. And I'd vote for anyone promising to protect jobs that need a human, like nursing and midwifery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a tight chest. I'd pray more. I'd want to hold on to what's familiar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandmother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't worry and I'll cook tonight. She'd say I should keep studying, and not worry about her. She survived worse. That's her answer to everything, and it helps a little, but I know she's frightened too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is two years different from the longer ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's no space to try things slowly. I'd have to decide now whether to keep going or to take a job. With a longer time, I'd wait and see what other people did first. Two years takes that away, and I'd hate that.

say: It's far too **fast** and nobody is prepared.
We must look after each other and not leave anyone behind.
think: Two years means I'm not even **qualified**, and my grandmother's pension and my uncle's restaurant could be shaken.
It feels like the ground is moving.
do: Keep on with the course and ask my uncle to promise me **shifts**.
Save every spare pound and ask my parents if I could go home if things got bad.
Vote for anyone who protects jobs that need a human.
feel: **Anxious** with a tight chest, wanting to hold on to what's familiar.
S2.quote: Two years takes that away, and I'd hate that.
fieldNote: Rosa's usual habit of waiting to see what others do is taken away by the **two-year** window.
She does not expect to lose her own job first, but she fears for her grandmother and uncle.

steps.text: Stay on the midwifery course and keep the Wednesday placement
Save every spare pound from the restaurant wage
Ask my parents if I can go home if things get bad
Vote for people promising to protect human jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to adapt if we're sensible. I'd tell friends not to panic but to stay in their jobs and learn. At the restaurant I'd say my uncle should think about a smaller menu and a few regulars, so it works either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel worried but steady. I'd qualify in about three years, and then I'd have a couple of years on the ward before robots come to hospitals. Midwifery needs a person in the room, so I think I'd be needed. I'd still save for a rainy day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the course, take a post at a hospital near home, and keep helping my grandmother. I'd put aside about fifty pounds a month once I'm paid. I'd learn the tools the hospital uses once other staff have. I'd also keep cooking with my grandmother, because it's a skill I want to hand on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but fine. It's like a long hill: you can see the top, and you keep walking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be in place when you qualify?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A permanent contract, a small savings pot and a hospital that's looked after the staff. I'd ask Bronagh which hospitals treat their midwives well, because the job matters less than the team. I'd rather be somewhere good than somewhere big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think about the robots coming three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd find it hard to imagine, a machine in a labour room. Mothers would want a human, I'm sure, but maybe machines would do the heavy lifting or the tests. I'd want to learn how, if it makes my work safer, once someone I trust has shown me.

say: Five years is enough to **adapt** if we're sensible.
I'd tell friends not to panic, but to stay in their jobs and learn.
think: I'd be worried but steady: about two years on the ward before **robots** come to hospitals.
Midwifery needs a person in the room, so I'd still be needed.
do: Finish the course and take a hospital **post** near home.
Put aside fifty pounds a month once I'm paid.
Learn the hospital's tools after other staff have.
feel: Anxious but fine, like a long **hill** where you see the top and keep walking.
S3.quote: I'd rather be somewhere good than somewhere big.
fieldNote: Rosa says the **team** matters more than the job and wants a hospital that treats its midwives well.
She imagines machines doing the heavy lifting or tests, but not replacing the human in a labour room.

steps.text: Finish the course and take a hospital post near home
Put aside fifty pounds a month once I'm paid
Learn the hospital's tools once other midwives have

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and I'd tell people it's not a reason to stop doing what you love. At the temple I'd say pass on skills to the young. At the restaurant, I'd say my uncle should train someone before he retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel quite calm. I'd be a midwife for years, maybe have my own family and have a bit of money. Robots would arrive when I'm about thirty-two. Ten years is long enough to get used to the thinking changes. The only thing I'd worry about is that the hospitals don't hire enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, work as a midwife and save for a small flat. I'd help my grandmother with her bills for as long as she's here. I'd learn the new tools when they've been proven. I'd probably work part time when I have children. And I'd keep cooking the recipes my grandmother taught me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady and warm, mostly. A little sad, because ten years is also the time when my grandmother gets older, and that's the thing I think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your grandmother figure in the ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'll be about eighty-five, and I'd want to be there for her, and I'd be glad of a job near home. I'd want to learn all the recipes before my grandmother can't teach them. It's the main thing that matters to me in the ten years, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently if you knew about the ten years in advance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy less and save more now. I'd learn to cook more of the family dishes. And I'd pick a hospital that looks after its people, so that when things shift, I'm in a team that sticks together.

say: Ten years is long, so it's not a reason to stop doing what you **love**.
Pass on skills to the young.
think: I'd feel quite **calm**, a midwife for years with robots arriving when I'm about thirty-two.
My only worry is that hospitals won't hire enough.
do: Finish the degree, work as a midwife and save for a small **flat**.
Help my grandmother with her bills and learn her recipes.
Learn new tools once they've been proven.
feel: Steady and warm, a little **sad** because my grandmother will be older.
S4.quote: I'd want to learn all the recipes before my grandmother can't teach them.
fieldNote: Rosa's long view is about **people**: her grandmother, the team she joins and the recipes she wants to learn.
She worries hospitals will not hire enough more than she worries about technology.

steps.text: Work as a midwife in a hospital that looks after its staff
Save for a small flat and help with my grandmother's bills
Learn my grandmother's recipes while she can still teach me

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Two years. That's the one where there's no space to wait and see, and I'd have to decide everything at once with no money. What would help is honest information, jobs that stay human, and a hospital or a college that looks after its students.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that the quiet ones, like me, who do the extra shifts and don't ask for anything, are the ones who get missed. I'd like somebody to ask us directly what we need.

headlineQuote: The quiet ones, like me, who do the extra shifts and don't ask for anything, are the ones who get missed.
portrait: Rosa is a 19-year-old **midwifery** student who lives with her grandmother and waits tables at her uncle's noodle restaurant.
She is traditional and steady: she follows proven tools, trusts mentors and prefers to see what others do first.
Her money worries are unpaid placements and a grandmother on a small pension, not AI.
Her answers stay close to people: her grandmother, her mentor, the team she wants to join.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most because it takes away the chance to wait and see.
whatWouldHelp: Honest information, jobs that stay **human**, and a college or hospital that looks after its students.
